claims.claim: Single-cell RNA-seq databases support the widespread expression pattern of Fshr.
claims.source: Finally, we also searched Fshr expression at single-cell level in four single-cell databases including DISCO (a database of Deeply Integrated Single-Cell Omics data, https://www.immunesinglecell.org/), BioGPS (a free extensible and customizable gene annotation portal, a complete resource for gene expression and protein function, http://biogps.org/exrna/#goto=welcome), Single Cell Portal (SCP, an interactive home for single-cell genomics data, https://singlecell.broadinstitute.org/), and Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx portal, https://gtexportal.org). The selected results from these databases are presented in Appendix 1—figure 3, which further support our findings of the widespread express pattern of Fshr described as above.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data from single-cell RNA-seq databases.

claims.claim: Fshr expression was detected in Leydig cells by scRNA-seq in DISCO and BioGPS for human cells.
claims.source: In particular, Fshr expression was detected in Leydig cells by scRNA-seq as seen in DISCO (https://immunesinglecell.org/genepage/FSHR) and BioGPS (http://biogps.org/#goto=genereport&id=2492) for human cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data from single-cell RNA-seq databases.

claims.claim: Fshr is not limited to previously reported cells, tissues, or organs, such as the reproductive system, osteoclasts, adipose, endothelium in tumors, and neurons in the brain, but rather has a wide expression in the cells, tissues, and organs in the body, particularly in the lung, kidney, and heart, as well as Leydig cells in the testis.
claims.source: Taken together, these data further confirmed Fshr-ZsGreen expression patterns from the Fshr-ZsGreen reporter line, convincingly demonstrating that Fshr is not limited to previously reported cells, tissues, or organs, such as the reproductive system, osteoclasts, adipose, endothelium in tumors, and neurons in the brain, but rather has a wide expression in the cells, tissues, and organs in the body, particularly in the lung, kidney, and heart, as well as Leydig cells in the testis, which has not previously been recognized.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: ZsGreen is an exceptionally bright green fluorescent protein derived from a Zoanthus sp. reef coral that has been modified for high solubility, bright emission, and rapid chromophore maturation.
claims.source: Because of its high turnover of Fshr mRNA and a difficulty in detection of Fshr expression by RT-PCR and northern blotting, in this reporter line, we utilized ZsG as a GFP reporter, as ZsGreen, also called ZsGreen1, is an exceptionally bright green fluorescent protein derived from a Zoanthus sp. reef coral (Matz et al., 1999) that has been modified for high solubility, bright emission, and rapid chromophore maturation.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about ZsGreen supported by a citation.

claims.claim: ZsGreen is the brightest commercially available green fluorescent protein - up to 4× brighter than EGFP with the half-life of 26 hr.
claims.source: ZsGreen is the brightest commercially available green fluorescent protein - up to 4× brighter than EGFP with the half-life of 26 hr - and is ideally suited for whole-cell labeling and promoter-reporter studies to indicate the promoter activity of a gene of interest, which has been used in numerous GFP reporter mice (Zhu et al., 2012b; Pippin et al., 2013; Pippin et al., 2014; Büller et al., 2015; Dewas et al., 2015; Nazareth et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2015; Kaverina et al., 2016; Saito et al., 2016; Fougère et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about ZsGreen supported by citations.

claims.claim: The 19-amino acid P2A has the highest cleavage efficiency.
claims.source: In addition, we also employed a short and conserved picornavirus-derived 'self-cleaving' 2A peptide to allow bicistronic expression of Fshr and ZsG, as the 19-amino acid P2A has the highest cleavage efficiency (Wang et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about P2A peptides supported by citations.

claims.claim: The cleavage of P2A is triggered by ribosomal skipping of the peptide bond between the proline (P) and glycine (G) in C-terminal of P2A peptide.
claims.source: The cleavage is triggered by ribosomal skipping of the peptide bond between the proline (P) and glycine (G) in C-terminal of P2A peptide, resulting in the peptide located upstream of the 2A peptide to have extra amino acids on its C-terminal end, while the peptide located downstream the 2A peptide will have an extra proline on its N-terminal end.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of P2A cleavage.

claims.claim: P2A can nearly equalize the expression of genes upstream and downstream.
claims.source: Therefore, P2A can nearly equalize the expression of genes upstream and downstream.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of P2A cleavage.

claims.claim: Fshr is normally expressed without interruptions and ZsG expression indicates Fshr promoter activity in the defined cells.
claims.source: As a result, Fshr is normally expressed without interruptions and ZsG expression indicates Fshr promoter activity in the defined cells, demonstrated by the comparison of Fshr expression in the testes and ovaries between Fshr-ZsGreen and B6 mice (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental validation shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: The P2A-ZsGreen construct was precisely inserted into the site between the last exon (exon 10) and the stop codon of the Fshr locus.
claims.source: The P2A-ZsGreen construct was precisely inserted into the site between the last exon (exon 10) and the stop codon of the Fshr locus, which was confirmed by integration detection PCR, sequencing of PCR fragments, and Southern blotting with Fshr locus-specific enzyme restriction digestions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental validation described in the methods and results.

claims.claim: Successful insertion allows the endogenous promoter of Fshr to drive ZsGreen reporter expression.
claims.source: Successful insertion allows the endogenous promoter of Fshr to drive ZsGreen reporter expression.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the design of the reporter construct.

claims.claim: Using the native regulatory element responsible for governing the expression of the target gene ensures that the expression pattern of the GFP reporter closely mirrors that of the gene of interest, Fshr, within its natural context.
claims.source: This approach greatly enhanced our understanding of this critical cellular pathway in several ways. First, employing the native regulatory element responsible for governing the expression of the target gene ensures that the expression pattern of the GFP reporter closely mirrors that of the gene of interest, Fshr, within its natural context. Consequently, this approach provides a more faithful representation of gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of using endogenous promoters.

claims.claim: Endogenous promoters often exhibit specific spatial and temporal expression patterns, driving gene expression in specific cell types or developmental stages.
claims.source: Second, endogenous promoters often exhibit specific spatial and temporal expression patterns, driving gene expression in specific cell types or developmental stages. This capability facilitates the capture of the dynamic nature of gene regulation and enables the study of gene expression under diverse physiological conditions.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about endogenous promoters.

claims.claim: Utilizing endogenous promoters minimizes potential perturbations to the native gene regulation machinery.
claims.source: Third, utilizing endogenous promoters minimizes potential perturbations to the native gene regulation machinery. It avoids the need to introduce exogenous elements or artificial constructs, reducing the likelihood of altering the gene's expression behavior or interfering with its regulatory interactions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of using endogenous promoters.

claims.claim: Using a tagged protein under endogenous regulation avoids fixation artifacts and allows detection of the target's activity in live cells.
claims.source: Unlike biochemical assays or immunostaining, using a tagged protein under endogenous regulation avoids fixation artifacts and allows detection of the target's activity in live cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the reporter system.

claims.claim: The findings of Fshr expression in Leydig cells are in line with previous works in fishes, rats, dogs, and humans performed by immunohistochemistry (IHC) and in situ hybridization.
claims.source: Although this finding is different from present thoughts that Fshr is only present in Sertoli cells but not in other cell types of the testis, our finding is in line with previous works in fishes (including African catfish, zebrafish, teleosts, and Japanese eels) (García-López et al., 2009; Levavi-Sivan et al., 2010; García-López et al., 2010; Burow et al., 2020; Chauvigné et al., 2012; Ohta et al., 2007, rats An et al., 2022), dogs (Kasimanickam and Kasimanickam, 2015), and humans (Bonci et al., 2018) performed by immunohistochemistry (IHC) and in situ hybridization.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: In humans, Fshr was highly expressed in Leydig cells.
claims.source: In humans, Fshr was also highly expressed in Leydig cells, although it was taken as non-specificity of the anti-Fshr antibodies.
claims.evidence: This is supported by previous research, though it was previously questioned.

claims.claim: The findings of Fshr expression in Leydig cells are supported by a report of the failure of normal Leydig cell development resulting from the deficiency of Fshr but not Fsh-beta.
claims.source: Furthermore, our findings are supported by a report of the failure of normal Leydig cell development resulting from the deficiency of Fshr but not Fsh-beta (Baker et al., 2003) and scRNA-seq studies in Hu sheep (originated from Mongolian sheep) (Su et al., 2023) and in human as shown in Appendix 1—figure 3 (DISCO, https://immunesinglecell.org/genepage/FSH) and BioGPS for human cells (http://biogps.org/#goto=genereport&id=2492).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and scRNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Fshr expression in Leydig cells strongly indicates that Fsh-Fshr plays a role in the production of steroids in males.
claims.source: Fshr expression in Leydig cells strongly indicates that Fsh-Fshr plays a role in the production of steroids in males.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed expression pattern and known functions of Leydig cells.

claims.claim: Leydig cell line TM3 expresses much lower Fshr compared to the Leydig cells in vivo.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, Leydig cell line TM3 expresses much lower Fshr, compared to the Leydig cells in vivo (Figure 2B–G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The low Fshr expression in TM3 cells may provide evidence on a reason that these cells do not respond well to FSH treatments.
claims.source: It may provide an evidence on a reason that these cells do not respond well to FSH treatments (Mather, 1980), and indicates that this cell line may not be a typical Leydig cell population and new Leydig cell lines should be established in the future.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed low Fshr expression in TM3 cells and their known poor response to FSH.

claims.claim: Fshr expression was observed in osteoclasts in frozen sections.
claims.source: In previous reports, Fshr expression in osteoclasts was detected only by RT-PCR, western blot, and immunostaining in cultures of primary murine precursors (Sun et al., 2006; Zhu et al., 2012a; Zhu et al., 2012c). Using the Fshr-ZsGreen reporter line, we visualized Fshr expression in multinucleated osteoclasts in frozen sections, clearly demonstrating Fshr expression in osteoclasts.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from the Fshr-ZsGreen reporter mice.

claims.claim: Fshr expression was observed in cells of the osteoblast lineage, from osteoprogenitor cells and osteoblasts to osteocytes and bone lining cells.
claims.source: Intriguingly, this powerful tool enabled us to examine Fshr expression in other cell types in bone. Surprisingly, we observed Fshr expression in cells of the osteoblast lineage, from osteoprogenitor cells and osteoblasts to osteocytes and bone lining cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from the Fshr-ZsGreen reporter mice.

claims.claim: Fsh may regulate not only osteoclast-mediated bone resorption but also osteoblasts for bone formation.
claims.source: This finding indicates that Fsh may regulate not only osteoclast-mediated bone resorption but also osteoblasts for bone formation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed Fshr expression in both osteoclasts and osteoblasts.

claims.claim: The Fshr cKO induced in osteocytes significantly reduced Fshr expression and triggered an increase in the cortical thickness.
claims.source: To functionally prove the presence of Fshr in osteoblasts/osteocytes, we also deleted Fshr in osteocytes in an inducible model. The Fshr cKO induced in osteocytes significantly reduce Fshr expression and triggered an increase in the cortical thickness (Figure 3D) and a much more profound increase in bone mass and a decrease in fat mass than blockade by Fsh antibodies (unpublished data), illuminating Fshr expression in the osteoblast lineage.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Bright Fshr-ZsGreen is more obviously seen in large arteries, such as the ascending aorta and others located in the heart.
claims.source: This bright Fshr-ZsGreen is more obviously seen in large arteries, such as the ascending aorta and others located in the heart.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from the Fshr-ZsGreen reporter mice.

claims.claim: Fshr was detected in vessels in solid malignant tumors by IHC or RT-PCR.
claims.source: Similarly, Fshr was detected in vessels in solid malignant tumors by IHC or RT-PCR (Abudureyimu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The highest Fshr-ZsGreen expression was detected in bronchial and bronchiole ciliated epithelial cells by both fluorescence microscopy and ddRT-PCR.
claims.source: Strikingly, we detected the highest Fshr-ZsGreen expression in bronchial and bronchiole ciliated epithelial cells by both fluorescence microscopy and ddRT-PCR.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from fluorescence microscopy and ddRT-PCR.

claims.claim: Fshr was more highly expressed in other cell types in the lung, such as type I pneumocytes (alveolar lining cells), type II pneumocytes (great alveolar or septal cells), and gland cells.
claims.source: It was also more highly expressed in other cell types in the lung, such as type I pneumocytes (alveolar lining cells), type II pneumocytes (great alveolar or septal cells), and gland cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from the Fshr-ZsGreen reporter mice.

claims.claim: The role of the unexpectedly high Fshr expression in the lung remains unknown.
claims.source: However, the role of this unexpectedly high Fshr expression in the lung remains unknown.
claims.evidence: This is a statement acknowledging the lack of functional understanding.

claims.claim: The second highest expression of Fshr-ZsGreen was found in renal epithelial cells in proximal and distal convoluted tubules but weak expression in renal corpuscles.
claims.source: Similarly, we also found the second highest expression of Fshr-ZsGreen in renal epithelial cells in proximal and distal convoluted tubules but weak expression in renal corpuscles.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from the Fshr-ZsGreen reporter mice.

claims.claim: The finding of Fshr expression in adipose tissues is consistent with the observations from previous works.
claims.source: In addition, our finding of Fshr expression in adipose tissues is consistent with the observations from previous works (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Fshr expression was reported to be present in β-cells of the pancreas to regulate glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
claims.source: Recently, Fshr expression was reported to be present in β-cells of the pancreas to regulate glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, further supporting our findings of the Fshr expression pattern (Cheng et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claims.claim: The Fshr-ZsGreen reporter line faithfully recapitulates endogenous Fshr expression at single-cell resolution.
claims.source: In summary, we established and validated an Fshr-ZsGreen protein reporter in vivo that faithfully recapitulates endogenous Fshr expression at single-cell resolution.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental validation data.

claims.claim: In addition to gonadal tissues, Fshr is also highly expressed in extragonadal systems, such as the lung, kidney, heart, and pancreas.
claims.source: Our compelling findings reveal that in addition to gonadal tissues, Fshr is also highly expressed in extragonadal systems, such as the lung, kidney, heart, and pancreas.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data.

claims.claim: The Fshr-ZsGreen reporter line is a powerful tool for detecting the location of Fshr expression.
claims.source: Although the Fshr-ZsGreen reporter line is a powerful tool for detecting the location of Fshr expression, it is limited in the definition of individual isoforms of Fshr transcripts and the detection of their turnover, which should be addressed by specific antibodies and determined by the rates of transcription and RNA degradation, including Xrn1 for 5'-to-3' degradation, exosomes for 3'-to-5' degradation, and nonsense-mediated decay (Wada and Becskei, 2017; Kaverina et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the reporter system.

results.result: The authors successfully generated Fshr-ZsGreen reporter mice using CRISPR-Cas9 technology by inserting a P2A-ZsGreen cassette before the stop codon of the Fshr gene. The P2A peptide enables bicistronic expression, allowing ZsGreen to report Fshr promoter activity without disrupting endogenous Fshr expression. The correct insertion was validated by PCR, sequencing, and Southern blotting in F0 and F1 generations, and the mice showed normal fertility and behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C42 provide comprehensive molecular and genetic validation of the reporter construct through multiple independent methods (PCR, sequencing, Southern blotting). The P2A system design (C37-C38, C129-C131) is well-established technology cited appropriately. Claim C42 confirms no obvious phenotypic abnormalities. The validation is thorough and the reporter design is sound.

results.result: The Fshr-ZsGreen reporter provides a reliable readout of endogenous Fshr expression at single-cell resolution. Validation by ddRT-PCR showed that Fshr expression levels in testes and ovaries were similar between Fshr-ZsGreen and wild-type B6 mice, confirming that the P2A-ZsGreen insertion did not disrupt endogenous Fshr expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 provide direct experimental validation using ddRT-PCR (Figure 2G) showing no significant difference in Fshr expression between reporter and wild-type mice in reproductive tissues. This is critical validation that the reporter faithfully reflects endogenous expression without disruption. The single-cell resolution capability (C5) is demonstrated throughout the imaging data.

results.result: Fshr-ZsGreen expression was observed throughout ovarian follicles at different developmental stages (primordial to corpus luteum), including oocytes, granulosa cells, theca cells, and ciliated epithelial cells in the oviduct. Colocalization with Stra8 confirmed expression in reproductive cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 are supported by comprehensive imaging data in Figure 2A showing Fshr-ZsGreen expression across multiple ovarian cell types and developmental stages. The colocalization with Stra8 (C46), a validated reproductive cell marker, provides independent confirmation of cell identity. The imaging is clear and well-documented.

results.result: Fshr is expressed in testicular Leydig cells, with strong expression demonstrated by Fshr-ZsGreen reporter, immunofluorescence with Set marker, and RNA-smFISH. This finding is consistent with previous reports in fish, rats, dogs, and humans, and is supported by scRNA-seq databases and functional studies showing Fshr deficiency affects Leydig cell development. TM3 Leydig cell line showed much lower Fshr expression than primary Leydig cells in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 provide multiple independent lines of evidence for Fshr expression in Leydig cells: reporter expression (Figure 2B), colocalization with Set marker (C49-C50), and RNA-smFISH validation (C52). Claims C139-C141 appropriately cite supporting literature from multiple species. The TM3 cell line observation (C143-C144) is supported by ddRT-PCR data (C58, Figure 2G) showing 145-fold lower expression than in vivo. This is a major finding challenging traditional views.

results.result: The TM3 Leydig cell line exhibited much lower Fshr expression (145-fold lower than testes, 3.6-fold lower than ovaries) compared to primary Leydig cells in vivo, with the majority of cells showing low Fshr staining and some nuclear localization observed. Fshr expression was significantly higher (40-fold) in testes compared to ovaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 2E), and C57-C58 are supported by quantitative ddRT-PCR data (Figure 2G). The nuclear localization observation (C54) is interesting but not extensively characterized. The low expression in TM3 cells is well-documented and may explain poor FSH responsiveness noted in C144.

results.result: FSHR expression in human Leydig cells was detected in single-cell RNA-seq databases (DISCO and BioGPS), and multiple scRNA-seq databases support the widespread expression pattern of Fshr across tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C125 are supported by database queries shown in Appendix 1-figure 3. Claim C124 references four different scRNA-seq databases. While database evidence is supportive, it relies on external data quality and annotation accuracy. The consistency across multiple databases strengthens the claim.

results.result: Fshr is expressed in multiple bone cell types including osteoblasts, osteoclasts, osteocytes, bone lining cells, and skeletal stem/progenitor cells. Expression was observed throughout the osteoblast lineage from progenitors to mature osteocytes embedded in bone matrix. Osteoclasts and osteoblasts were confirmed by colocalization with Trap and osteocalcin markers, respectively. Stem/progenitor cells were identified using CD34 and CD133 markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C67 are extensively supported by imaging data in Figure 3A-C with appropriate cell-type specific markers (osteocalcin for osteoblasts, Trap for osteoclasts, CD34/CD133 for stem cells). The observation of Fshr in osteoblast lineage cells (C146) is novel and well-documented. Previous reports only showed osteoclast expression (C145), making the osteoblast lineage finding particularly significant.

results.result: Osteocyte-specific conditional knockout of Fshr (using DMP1-CreERT2) significantly reduced Fshr expression in osteocytes and increased cortical bone thickness, providing functional evidence for Fshr expression and activity in osteocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 are supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3D showing reduced Fshr expression and increased cortical thickness in cKO mice. This provides functional validation of Fshr expression in osteocytes. However, C148 mentions unpublished data on bone mass and fat mass changes, which cannot be fully evaluated. The presented data on cortical thickness is clear and convincing.

results.result: Fshr-ZsGreen is expressed in white and brown adipose tissues, including adipocyte membranes and cytoplasm, arterioles, and peripheral neural fibers. In WAT, Fshr colocalized with Ucp1 in two distinct adipocyte populations. In BAT, Fshr was expressed in brown adipocytes and peripheral nerve fibers (TH+ and Peri+), including nodes of Ranvier. Expression patterns were confirmed by Fshr antibody staining in B6 mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C79 are comprehensively supported by imaging data in Figures 4A-G with multiple markers (Ucp1, TH, Peri). The identification of two Fshr+ adipocyte populations (C71) and expression in peripheral nerves (C75-C78) is well-documented. Independent validation with Fshr antibody in B6 mice (C79, C156) strengthens the findings. Consistent with prior literature (C156).

results.result: Fshr is expressed in cardiovascular tissues including cardiomyocytes, endothelial cells, and smooth muscle cells of the heart and large arteries. Expression was observed in all three layers of blood vessels (tunica intima, media, and adventitia), with particularly bright expression in large arteries like the ascending aorta. Colocalization with α-SMA and EMCN confirmed cell identities. Brown adipose tissue and neural fiber clusters were also observed around cardiac vessels.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C93 are extensively supported by detailed imaging in Figures 5A-D using multiple markers (α-SMA, EMCN). The systematic examination of different vessel types and layers is thorough. The observation of differential α-SMA staining intensity in different smooth muscle layers (C90) adds detail. Expression in endothelial cells (C8) is a major finding given the widespread vasculature.

results.result: Fshr shows the highest expression in lung epithelial cells, particularly in bronchial and bronchiole ciliated epithelium, bronchial glands, and alveolar type I and II cells. This was confirmed by both fluorescence microscopy and ddRT-PCR showing lung as the highest expressing tissue. Colocalization with PD-L1 confirmed respiratory cell identity. The functional role of this high expression remains unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C98 are supported by extensive imaging in Figure 6A with PD-L1 colocalization. Claims C121 and C152 provide quantitative validation by ddRT-PCR (Figure 14B) showing lung has the highest Fshr expression among all tissues examined. The acknowledgment that functional significance is unknown (C154) is appropriate. This is a striking and novel finding.

results.result: Fshr shows the second highest expression in kidney, with high expression in proximal and distal convoluted tubule epithelial cells but weak expression in glomerular capillaries. Expression was also observed in arteriolar endothelium. This was confirmed by ddRT-PCR showing kidney as the second highest expressing tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 are supported by imaging data in Figure 6B with Col1a1 colocalization. The differential expression between tubules (high) and glomeruli (weak) is clearly shown. Claims C121 and C155 provide quantitative validation by ddRT-PCR. The kidney finding is well-documented and represents a major discovery.

results.result: Fshr-ZsGreen is expressed in liver hepatocytes and arteries, with colocalization with Col1a1 and CD31. Expression was observed in peripheral nerve fibers, being weak in large nerve fibers but strong in small neural fibers colocalizing with KCNMA1.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 are supported by imaging data in Figures 7A-C with appropriate markers. The differential expression in large versus small nerve fibers (C104) is an interesting detail. The liver findings are adequately documented though less extensively characterized than other organs.

results.result: Fshr-ZsGreen is expressed in pancreatic acinar cells and islets of Langerhans, including both α-cells and β-cells, confirmed by colocalization with NG3, insulin, and glucagon markers. Recent reports support Fshr expression in β-cells regulating glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C106 are supported by comprehensive imaging in Figures 8A-C with multiple cell-type specific markers. The identification of expression in both α- and β-cells is well-documented. Claim C157 appropriately cites recent supporting literature. The pancreatic findings are thorough and well-validated.

results.result: Fshr-ZsGreen is expressed in thyroid follicular cells and parafollicular cells (C-cells). Follicular cells showed positive nuclear staining for Tshr, confirming cell identity.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 are supported by imaging data in Figure 9 with Tshr colocalization. The identification of both follicular and parafollicular cell expression is clear. The nuclear Tshr staining pattern is noted but not extensively discussed.

results.result: Fshr-ZsGreen is expressed in skin including hair follicles, sweat glands, dermal and hypodermal fibroblasts, and epidermal keratinocytes. CD34+ stem/progenitor cells in the hair follicle bulge, dermal papilla, and epidermis colocalized with Fshr-ZsGreen.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by imaging data in Figures 10A-B. The colocalization with CD34 (C111) identifies stem/progenitor cell populations in multiple skin compartments. The skin findings are adequately documented with appropriate markers.

results.result: Fshr-ZsGreen is expressed in skeletal muscle fibers (with heterogeneous expression levels), satellite cells (colocalized with α-SMA and PAX7), and peripheral nerve fibers around vascular structures (identified by TH staining).
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C114 are supported by imaging data in Figure 11 with multiple markers. The identification of satellite cells using both α-SMA and PAX7 is thorough. The observation of heterogeneous expression in muscle fibers (C112) is noted but not extensively characterized.

results.result: Fshr is expressed in immune cells of the spleen and bone marrow, including myeloid-lineage cells (monocytes/macrophages, neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils), lymphoid cells (NK cells, B-cells, T-cells), identified by colocalization with CD11b, CD3, and F4/80 markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 are supported by imaging data in Figures 12A-C with appropriate immune cell markers. The identification of multiple immune cell types is comprehensive. The use of CD11b, CD3, and F4/80 markers is appropriate for the claimed cell types.

results.result: Fshr is expressed in brain cells including astrocytes, microglia, and neurons, as well as neuronal fibers (synapses or projections), demonstrated in olfactory bulbs, pallidum, and hippocampus.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 is supported by imaging data in Figure 13 showing colocalization with GFAP (astrocytes), Iba1 (microglia), and NeuN (neurons). The brain expression is documented in multiple regions. This represents an important finding for extragonadal Fshr expression.

results.result: Fshr expression was validated across all examined tissues by immunofluorescence with Fshr antibody showing colocalization with Fshr-ZsGreen, and by ddRT-PCR demonstrating Fshr mRNA in all tissues with three expression level categories: high (lung, kidney), moderate (bone, liver, muscle, etc.), and low (adipose, brain, pancreas, etc.).
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C123 provide comprehensive validation using two independent methods: Fshr antibody IF (Figure 14A) and ddRT-PCR (Figure 14B). The quantitative categorization of expression levels (C121-C123) is supported by the ddRT-PCR data. This validation across multiple tissues strengthens all tissue-specific findings.

results.result: Fshr expression is not limited to reproductive tissues but is widely expressed throughout the body, particularly in lung, kidney, heart, Leydig cells, osteoblast lineage cells, endothelial cells, and epithelial cells in multiple organs, challenging previous understanding of Fshr localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C126 and C159 represent the major conclusion synthesizing all experimental findings. These summary claims are well-supported by the comprehensive tissue survey using multiple validation methods (reporter expression, IF, ddRT-PCR, RNA-smFISH, scRNA-seq databases). The widespread expression pattern is convincingly demonstrated across reproductive and non-reproductive tissues.

results.result: Conventional methods for examining FSHR expression have limitations due to antibody non-specificity concerns and quick turnover/rapid degradation of Fshr transcripts. A GFP reporter driven by endogenous Fshr promoter can overcome these limitations by enabling visualization of low-abundance transcripts in more accurate and context-specific ways.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are supported by appropriate citations discussing methodological limitations in the field. Claim C35 is supported by citations on GFP reporter advantages. Claim C3 is an inference that appropriately motivates the study design. The rationale for developing the reporter system is well-justified.

results.result: Using the endogenous Fshr promoter to drive reporter expression ensures faithful representation of native gene expression patterns, captures spatial and temporal dynamics, minimizes perturbations to gene regulation, and avoids fixation artifacts compared to other methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C138 describe well-established advantages of endogenous promoter-driven reporters. These are appropriately presented as inferences about the methodological approach. The advantages are validated by the experimental data showing no disruption of endogenous Fshr expression (C55-C56).

results.result: The observation of Fshr expression in both osteoclasts and osteoblast lineage cells suggests that FSH may regulate both bone resorption and bone formation. Fshr expression in Leydig cells indicates FSH-FSHR plays a role in steroid production in males.
results.evaluation: Claims C147 and C142 are functional inferences based on expression patterns. While the expression data is solid, these claims about functional roles are speculative without direct functional studies. The conditional knockout data (C148) provides some functional support for osteocytes, but broader functional validation would be needed to fully support these mechanistic claims.

results.result: The Fshr-ZsGreen reporter line is a powerful tool for detecting Fshr expression location but has limitations in defining individual transcript isoforms and detecting their turnover, which requires specific antibodies and measurement of transcription and RNA degradation rates.
results.evaluation: Claim C160 appropriately acknowledges the limitations of the reporter system. This is a fair assessment that the reporter indicates promoter activity and protein localization but cannot distinguish between transcript isoforms or measure mRNA dynamics. The acknowledgment of limitations is scientifically appropriate.

results.result: The authors developed Fshr-ZsGreen reporter mice using CRISPR-Cas9 to insert a P2A-ZsGreen cassette before the stop codon of the Fshr gene. This design allows ZsGreen expression under the control of the endogenous Fshr promoter without disrupting Fshr expression, as validated by PCR, sequencing, Southern blotting, and ddRT-PCR showing similar Fshr expression in testes and ovaries between Fshr-ZsGreen and wild-type mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised fundamental concerns about the reporter system. One reviewer noted that 'the turnover of fluorescent proteins is long, longer than 48h, which means that they accumulate at a different speed than the endogenous Fshr,' questioning whether ZsGreen accumulation reflects actual Fshr protein levels. The reviewer also stated 'the entire manuscript is based on a single founder mouse, which is not acceptable' and that 'additional integrations cannot be detected by such' methods as Southern blots and PCR. The editor acknowledged the approach as 'novel and interesting' but noted 'additional validation of the localization data would strengthen the study considerably.'

results.result: The authors report strong Fshr expression in Leydig cells of the testis, with expression levels approximately 40-fold higher in testes compared to ovaries. This finding was supported by Fshr-ZsGreen reporter expression, immunofluorescence with Stra8 and Set markers, RNA-smFISH, and single-cell RNA-seq databases showing FSHR expression in human Leydig cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly challenged this finding. One reviewer stated 'Leydig cells cannot simply express more Fshr than Sertoli cells, that would go against what we have known for >50 years in physiology' and noted 'to make extraordinary claims there is a need for extraordinary evidence.' The reviewer found it 'disturbing' that 'the expression of ZsGreen in Leydig cells seems much higher than in Sertoli cells' and questioned whether 'even the tails of spermatozoa glow! This is not cytoplasm and cannot contain a soluble fluorescent protein.' The reviewer also noted that 'no single acceptable antibody against FSHR recognises Leydig cells' and that the claim of direct FSHR effects on Leydig cells rather than via Sertoli cell cross-talk is 'too much of a claim.'

results.result: The authors report Fshr expression in osteoblast lineage cells (osteoprogenitor cells, osteoblasts, osteocytes, and bone lining cells) in addition to osteoclasts. Conditional knockout of Fshr in osteocytes resulted in reduced Fshr expression and increased cortical thickness, suggesting functional relevance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the finding but questioned its validation. One reviewer noted 'One of the shocking observations in this manuscript is the expression of Fshr in...osteoblasts' and stated that the conditional knockout data 'would be a good control for all their images. I think it is necessary to make the large claim of extragonadal expression.' The editor noted that 'additional validation of the localization data would strengthen the study considerably.' The unpublished functional data on bone mass changes was mentioned but not available for review, limiting the ability to fully evaluate the functional significance.

results.result: The authors report Fshr expression in endothelial cells of vascular structures throughout the body, including in the heart, large arteries (ascending aorta), veins, and arterioles. Expression was confirmed by colocalization with endothelial markers α-SMA and EMCN.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about the specificity of the findings. One reviewer noted that 'the stainings of the aorta show the ZsGreen expression where elastin and collagen fibres are - these are not "cells" and therefore are not expressing ZsGreen,' questioning whether the signal represents true cellular expression. The reviewer also noted inconsistencies: 'In Fig 5, the section of aorta shows low staining in the elastin/collagen fibres, while there is clearly in Suppl Data 2.' The editor acknowledged the findings but emphasized that 'additional validation of the localization data would strengthen the study considerably.'

results.result: The authors report the highest Fshr expression in bronchial and bronchiole ciliated epithelial cells of the lung, as well as in type I and II pneumocytes, bronchial glands, and alveoli. This was confirmed by both fluorescence microscopy and ddRT-PCR showing high expression in lung tissue.
results.evaluation: Reviewers questioned the validity of this finding. One reviewer noted that 'the 2nd lung images show green fluorescence in the mucosa (centre) which should not be as there is no cells there,' suggesting non-specific signal. The reviewer also pointed out that 'in the datasets presented organs like "ovary" have almost no Fshr expression, which should question the validity of such' findings when single-cell data doesn't fully support the claims. The functional significance remains unknown as the authors acknowledge 'the role of this unexpectedly high Fshr expression in the lung remains unknown.'

results.result: The authors report the second highest Fshr expression in renal epithelial cells of proximal and distal convoluted tubules, with weaker expression in glomerular capillaries. This was confirmed by both fluorescence microscopy and ddRT-PCR.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not specifically address kidney findings in detail, but general concerns about validation apply. One reviewer noted that single-cell datasets show inconsistencies, and that 'many other cell types that show no expression such as hepatocytes and skeletal muscle, where the authors claim to have high expression of Fshr' raises questions about the reliability of the reporter system. The editor's comment that 'additional validation of the localization data would strengthen the study considerably' applies to these findings.

results.result: The authors report Fshr expression in white and brown adipose tissue, including in adipocyte membranes and cytoplasm, arterioles, and peripheral neural fibers. Expression was confirmed by colocalization with Ucp1, TH, and Peri markers, and by immunofluorescence in B6 mice showing similar patterns.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly questioned these findings. One reviewer stated 'The expression in WAT and BAT is also questionable as the expression of ZsGreen is high everywhere. What makes it difficult to actually believe that the images are truly informative?' The reviewer also noted that 'The detection of Fshr in e.g. adipocytes of B6 mice is as questionable as many other claims of gonadotropin receptors in extragonadal tissues, which has been questioned a number of times by many researchers.' The concern about ZsGreen accumulation versus actual Fshr protein expression is particularly relevant here.

results.result: The authors report widespread Fshr expression across multiple organs and tissues including liver, pancreas (α- and β-cells), thyroid, skin, skeletal muscle, spleen, bone marrow immune cells, and brain (astrocytes, microglia, neurons). This was supported by immunofluorescence colocalization with tissue-specific markers, ddRT-PCR showing expression in all examined tissues, and single-cell RNA-seq database searches.
results.evaluation: Reviewers fundamentally questioned the breadth of expression. One reviewer asked 'is there any tissue on these mice that does not "express" (Fshr)-ZsGreen? Because from what I see every single tissue analysed has "Fshr". Which might be the problem why it is so difficult to find.' The reviewer noted that 'virtually every cell in the provided tissues, and not only cells but structures, glows green' and that 'the additional single-cell data does not truly support their claims' as 'there are many other cell types that show no expression such as hepatocytes and skeletal muscle, where the authors claim to have high expression of Fshr.' The concern about ZsGreen accumulation artifacts and the use of a single founder mouse line undermines confidence in these widespread expression claims.

results.result: The authors conclude that the Fshr-ZsGreen reporter line faithfully recapitulates endogenous Fshr expression at single-cell resolution and demonstrates that Fshr has wide expression beyond previously reported tissues, particularly in lung, kidney, heart, and Leydig cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers rejected the overall conclusion. One reviewer stated 'The response by the authors does not seem sufficient or adequate, by any length, for what one would expect for a work having such a large claim as the expression of the Fshr in multiple cell types and organs.' The fundamental concerns about ZsGreen accumulation artifacts, use of a single founder mouse, lack of proper controls (WT and KI tissues side-by-side), and inconsistencies with single-cell RNA-seq data undermine the central claim that the reporter 'faithfully recapitulates' endogenous Fshr expression. The editor's assessment that the findings are 'valuable' but require 'additional validation' indicates the evidence is currently insufficient to support the broad conclusions.

results.result: The authors report Fshr-ZsGreen expression in ovarian follicles at different developmental stages (primordial to secondary follicles and corpus luteum), including in oocytes, granulosa cells, theca cells, and ciliated epithelial cells of the oviduct, with colocalization with Stra8 marker.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the ovarian expression findings, which align with established knowledge about FSHR expression in female reproductive tissues. The editor noted the findings help 'elucidate the expression and function of the FSH receptor' in gonadal tissues. However, one reviewer noted inconsistency with single-cell databases where 'organs like "ovary" have almost no Fshr expression,' though this may reflect database limitations rather than invalidating the primary data.

results.result: The authors provide background on FSH-FSHR biology, including established roles in reproduction, emerging evidence of extragonadal expression, ongoing debates about extragonadal functions, and methodological limitations of conventional approaches (antibody non-specificity, rapid mRNA turnover) that motivated development of the reporter system.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged these background points. One reviewer stated 'The authors are correct in that there is a lack of reliable antibodies against many of the GPCR family members' and that 'There has been a very long debate about the expression of gonadotropin receptors in other tissues other than gonads.' The reviewer also confirmed that 'one of the very first statements in the manuscript is that antibodies against GPCRs in general, and gonadotropin receptors more specifically, are unreliable.' These contextual claims about the field and methodological challenges were not disputed.

comparisons.comparison: Both address reporter construct validation (C36-C42, C127-C134) and endogenous expression validation (C55-C56, C132). OpenEval finds the validation comprehensive and thorough (SUPPORTED), while peer reviewers raise fundamental concerns about ZsGreen protein accumulation kinetics, use of a single founder mouse, and potential undetected additional integrations (UNCERTAIN).

OpenEval evaluates Fshr expression validation (C55-C56, C132) as SUPPORTED with ddRT-PCR data. Peer reviewers include these claims in their broader UNCERTAIN evaluation of the reporter system, questioning whether ZsGreen accumulation reflects actual Fshr protein levels.

Both address ovarian Fshr expression (C43-C46). OpenEval finds the imaging data and Stra8 colocalization convincing (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers also support these findings (SUPPORTED), noting they align with established knowledge, though they mention inconsistencies with single-cell databases.

Both evaluate Leydig cell Fshr expression (C47-C52, C139-C144). OpenEval finds multiple independent lines of evidence convincing (SUPPORTED), calling it a major finding. Peer reviewers strongly challenge this (UNSUPPORTED), stating it contradicts 50+ years of physiology, questioning the extraordinary claim, noting no acceptable antibody recognizes Leydig cells, and expressing concern about signal in sperm tails.

OpenEval evaluates testicular expression data (C53-C54, C57-C58) as SUPPORTED by immunofluorescence and ddRT-PCR. Peer reviewers include these claims in their UNSUPPORTED evaluation of Leydig cell expression, questioning the validity of the findings.

OpenEval finds database evidence (C59, C124-C125) SUPPORTED across multiple scRNA-seq databases. Peer reviewers note inconsistencies where single-cell datasets show low or no Fshr expression in organs where the reporter shows high expression, undermining confidence in the findings.
